name: Awya
confidence_why: The only statement on Awyi stress is a 1912 wordlist questionnaire filled in by Lieutenant N. Binnendijk and published in Stokhof (1983), which says stress falls 'mainly on the penultimate syllable or final syllable'; Voorhoeve (1971, 1975), the only linguist to describe the language, says nothing about stress, so the record rests on one unconfirmed non-specialist note whose list is tied to Awyi only by lexical similarity.
catalog_citation: Stokhof, W. A. L. (ed.) 1983. Holle Lists: Vocabularies in languages of Indonesia, Vol. 5/2: Irian Jaya: Papuan languages, Northern languages, Central Highlands languages (Pacific Linguistics D-53; Materials in Languages of Indonesia No. 19). Canberra: ANU. Holle list 133a 'Awya', collected by 1st Lieutenant N. Binnendijk, received NBG 1912.
catalog_locator: Holle list 133a AWYA, section 1 'General information', 1.2 'Other details', 1.2.1, p. 141 (verified; -> that folder). Awya wordlist pp. 142-146, notes pp. 146-147; Kwime list 133b p. 149 refers back to 133a.
catalog_quote: 1.2.1. The stress falls mainly on the penultimate syllable or final syllable. 1.2.2. This questionnaire contains two sets of words: Awya 133a and Kwime 133b. Items in 133a and 133b show a certain similarity with the so-called Taikat Family; see lists 101 (Awyi) and 102 (Taikat (Arso)) in Voorhoeve 1975, p. 43, 112.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no prior stress statement for Awyi; Voorhoeve 1971 (pp. 62-64) is silent on stress and Voorhoeve 1975 (p. 92) explicitly does not mark it. This is the first statement located: stress is penultimate or final, unresolved between the two. Section 1.2.2 (same page) says the list 'shows a certain similarity with the so-called Taikat Family; see lists 101 (Awyi) and 102 (Taikat (Arso)) in Voorhoeve 1975, p. 43, 112', so the compilers himself ties it to Awyi only tentatively. Lexical checks support the identification: Holle Awya 130 'wobio' matches Voorhoeve 1975 Awyi 'water' wobia (Taikat obea), and Holle Awya 1293-1302 'nanggar(e)' matches Awyi naŋger ('head'/'two')…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is reported to fall usually on the penultimate or on the final syllable, with no rule given for choosing between the two; this is a one-line remark attached to a 1912 military-exploration questionnaire (collected by 1st Lt. N. Binnendijk, received NBG 1912), not a phonological analysis. It excludes initial stress in longer words but does not decide between penult and final placement.
new_statements.exceptions: 'mainly' signals that some words deviate; no examples or conditions given. The wordlist itself (pp. 142-146) carries no stress marks.
new_statements.identity_note: The Holle list is labelled 'Awya' (list 133a), collected in 1912 by 1st Lt. N. Binnendijk during the Netherlands New Guinea military exploration; the companion list 133b is 'Kwime'. Stokhof (p. 141, 1.2.2) links both only tentatively to Awyi (Voorhoeve 1975 list 101) and Taikat/Arso (list 102). The name matches Glottolog's alternate name 'Awye' for awyi1241 and the lexical matches noted above (wobio ~ wobia 'water', nanggar ~ naŋger) make the identification with Awyi probable, but the 1912 list could represent a neighbouring Border variety (Taikat/Arso area); the stress remark should be recorded as pertaining to the 1912 'Awya' list, identified with Awyi with medium confidence.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Languages of Irian Jaya: Checklist. Preliminary classification, language maps, wordlists (Pacific Linguistics B-31). Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Entry no. 101 'Awyi (Njao)' p. 43: c. 200 speakers, villages Nyao, Yosko, Sowyo, Bukisom; sources Galis 1955, Cowan 1957b, Voorhoeve 1971, Laycock 1973. Wordlist conventions p. 92 state explicitly that 'lengthening of vowel, stress and pitch are not indicated'; Awyi 40-item list p. 112f. Silent on stress by design.

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1971. Miscellaneous notes on languages in West Irian, New Guinea. In T. Dutton et al., Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 14 (Pacific Linguistics A-28), 47-114. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Section 2.3.3 'Phonology' (pp. 62-64) treats Awji, Taikat, Manem, Waris together: stop/nasal places, 6 vowels + possible /E/, Awji aspiration, prenasalisation, /l/ allophones, distinctive nasal vowels, cluster phonotactics. Nothing on stress or accent for Awji (or any Tami-stock language). Appendix I comparative wordlist (p. 98ff) gives the Awji column with no stress or pitch marks (only the tonal Sko/Tumawo column carries pitch diacritics). Stress statements elsewhere in the paper concern Morwap (p. 72), Dera (2.5.3.1) and Sawuy, not Awji.

Lexicon (144 items) from Voorhoeve 1971 and 1975 only; no prosodic information; confirms no other sources are known to that database.
